hints: Add up the percentages yourself for short (4-12 + 14 + 16) and long (18 + >18) separately for cow and for whale. Which milk has much more of the very long >18 type?
Remember that a longer fatty acid chain has more C-H bonds to break in respiration, so it releases more energy. Link this to the fact that newborn whales grow faster and need more energy.
walkthrough:
**Work out what short and long mean**

First, group the table correctly. Short is 4 to 16 carbons, long is 18 or more carbons.

For cow: short = 22.2 + 10.6 + 25.5 = 58.3%, long = 40.1 + 1.6 = 41.7%.

For whale: short = 0 + 13.8 + 27.9 = 41.7%, long = 29.4 + 28.9 = 58.3%.

**Compare the short to long ratios**

Now compare short divided by long.

$$\text{cow ratio} = \frac{58.3}{41.7} \approx 1.40$$
$$\text{whale ratio} = \frac{41.7}{58.3} \approx 0.72$$

So the ratio in whale milk is lower than in cow milk. The cow milk is richer in short chains, the whale milk is richer in long chains, especially >18.

**Link chain length to energy need**

Longer saturated fatty acids contain more carbon and hydrogen atoms, so more bonds can be oxidised in respiration to release more ATP per molecule.

Newborn whales grow faster than newborn cows, so they need more energy. It makes sense their milk provides more long, energy-rich fatty acids, giving a lower short to long ratio.

options.A: The first half is true, the cow ratio is higher, but the reason is backwards. Young cows grow more slowly and need less energy than young whales.
options.B: The calculation is wrong. Cow short total (58.3%) is greater than whale short total (41.7%), so the cow ratio is higher, not lower.
options.C: The calculation is wrong. Whale milk has more long chains (58.3%), so its short to long ratio is lower, not higher.
options.D: Correct. Whale short to long ratio (about 0.72) is lower than cow (about 1.40) because fast-growing whales need more energy from longer, energy-rich fatty acids.
